content: Certain items are not considered cost-effective for all healthcare facilities at a given level, particularly in resource-limited settings. As a result, these items are not classified as essential. However, in countries with better resource availability, these items may eventually be deemed essential in their national healthcare plans. Similarly, some services require only low-cost physical resources and feasible training for healthcare personnel at the relevant level. Individual countries may choose to upgrade these services to essential, either universally or at facilities with high trauma volumes. In resource-poor environments, some trauma treatment capabilities may need to be shifted to lower levels of the healthcare system to improve availability. This shift typically involves minimal additional costs compared to providing these services only at higher levels. However, this often means that less specialized providers perform procedures typically handled by more highly trained personnel. It is important to note that the designation possibly required (PR) differs from desirable. PR indicates a potential necessity to expand trauma care services in resource-limited settings, primarily in low-income countries, but not in middle-income ones. Irrelevant (I) resources refer to capabilities that are not expected at a given level of the healthcare system, even with full resource availability. When developing national trauma plans, countries may appropriately reclassify some desirable items as essential. However, items designated as essential should remain so, except in extreme or unusual circumstances, as downgrading them could compromise trauma care below the Essential Trauma Care (EsTC) standard. While the guidelines provide detailed information on essential care elements, desirable items are also integral to the guidelines. Although they are considered less critical or cost-effective than essential items, they should not be ignored. Essential items are those that should be guaranteed for all injured patients at all facilities of a given level, even in low-income countries, such as village health posts, small hospitals without surgical capabilities, general practitioner (GP) hospitals, specialist hospitals with general surgeons, and tertiary care facilities with limited subspecialties. Many desirable items may be applicable to facilities in middle-income countries or those with high trauma patient volumes. At the basic level, the focus is on rapid, basic first aid. In national plans addressing the basic level, some items may be upgraded to essential for higher-level basic facilities, such as those staffed by nurses or medical assistants. At all levels of the healthcare system, it is essential for healthcare personnel to recognize signs of airway obstruction and be skilled in manual maneuvers to maintain airway patency while protecting the cervical spine. The success of airway management increases with the availability of specific equipment and the skills to use it safely, including oral airways, suction devices, and bag-valve-mask ventilation. These are essential at hospital-level facilities. Advanced airway management, such as endotracheal intubation and cricothyroidotomy, is essential at specialist-staffed hospitals. However, the need for resources and the potential for harm increase with advanced airway management. In resource-rich environments or facilities with high trauma volumes, it may be appropriate to reclassify desirable items as essential at certain facilities. Safety assurances, such as readily available equipment and adequately trained staff, are critical for successful procedures. Suction devices, including manual or foot pump devices and stiff suction tips, are essential in any hospital. A basic trauma pack containing essential instruments and supplies is also critical for smaller procedures in emergency settings. Cricothyroidotomy is the preferred surgical airway in emergencies and can be performed quickly, often transitioning to a tracheostomy if needed for prolonged periods. The ability to assess respiratory distress and ventilation adequacy is essential at all healthcare levels, requiring only training and a stethoscope. Oxygen administration capabilities are essential at all hospital facilities but may not be feasible for most primary care clinics in low-income countries. Recognizing and treating tension pneumothorax with needle thoracostomy and tube thoracostomy is essential at all hospital-level facilities. Basic-level facilities may consider temporary relief with needle thoracostomy desirable if rapid evacuation to definitive care is possible. Recognizing sucking chest wounds and applying three-way dressings are essential at all levels. Advanced monitoring and laboratory tests, such as arterial blood gases and oxygen saturation, are desirable but not essential due to cost constraints. Training on arterial tourniquet use in extreme situations and splinting fractured extremities to reduce internal bleeding is essential. Fluid resuscitation capabilities, including equipment, fluids, and skills, are essential at all hospital levels. Peripheral intravenous access and crystalloid use are essential, while central lines are essential at higher hospital levels and desirable at GP-level hospitals. Blood transfusion capabilities are essential at all hospital levels, with formal blood banks preferred. Immediate donation and administration of fresh whole blood are acceptable alternatives. Clinicians must understand transfusion indications, monitor patient responses, and recognize complications. Laboratory tests, such as hematocrit or hemoglobin monitoring, are essential, while advanced tests like electrolytes and arterial blood gases are desirable. Recognizing and treating hypothermia with external rewarming is essential at all levels. Providing warmed fluids and other core rewarming methods is desirable. Weighing scales for children to calculate fluid requirements are essential at hospital levels and desirable at the basic level. These guidelines emphasize the need for specific skills, equipment, and supplies to address life-threatening injuries during initial evaluation and management. While operating theatre details are beyond the scope of this publication, the guidelines outline the services that should be provided, implying the necessary training, equipment, and supplies are available.
